newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil govt confident ahead of re-election vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil govt confident ahead of re-election vote.

text.p: The Brazilian government is confident it will win a comfortable majority Wednesday afternoon when the Senate votes on a bill that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to seek re-election, officials said.
"The vote is scheduled for this afternoon. The government thinks it will be tranquil," said an aide to Senator Jose Roberto Arruda, the government's leader in Congress.

The aide said Arruda had played host to several senators and government leaders at a dinner Tuesday night and the consensus was that the re-election bill would pass with 59 votes, 10 more than the minimum three-fifths majority needed.
The Senate session was due to start at 1430 local/1330 EDT/1730 GMT with voting itself expected to kick off an hour later.

Senators themselves considering running in the next gubernatorial polls had been insisting on changes to the bill to force sitting governors and mayors to step down six months before seeking re-election.

But the government struck a deal and the senators were expected to approve the same bill that has already passed through the lower house in order to avoid the necessity of having to send the law back to the Chamber.
"If we change the bill and it has to go back to the Chamber, what with all the furor at the moment in the lower house it will never again come back out," Arruda's aide said.

The lower house has been rocked by allegations at least five deputies were bribed by the governors of Acre and Amazonas states to vote in favour of re-election. The allegations drew swift denials of wrongdoing from the politicians named by a newspaper as being involved in the purported scheme.
Officials said that the government's lawyers had found an already existing law they said would require governors and mayors to step down before re-election.
They said the up to 30 senators eyeing governorships had accepted the lawyer's report as sufficient guarantee they would not be at a disadvantage to the incumbents if they decide to run.
